original_question: Determine how fast the sequences {ms([n], r)}_{n=1}^{∞} and {bms([n], r)}_{n=1}^{∞} converge to their common limit ms([0, 1], r).
target_in_paper: Section 8, Question 8.5 of the survey. Its exact formulation is the question: "How quickly the sequences {ms([n],r)} and {bms([n],r)} converge to their limit ms([0,1],r)?" The sharper source-level version behind this survey question asks, in particular, whether |ms([n],r)-ms([0,1],r)| = O(1/n^alpha) for some alpha>0, and how much faster bms([n],r) converges. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right object, the right ambient spaces, and the right asymptotic direction: it asks about the two sequences ms([n],r) and bms([n],r), recognizes that they have the common limit ms([0,1],r), and asks for the rate of convergence as n -> infinity. That is essentially the content of Section 8, Question 8.5. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))
missing_details: The paper treats r as a fixed positive integer, i.e. a fixed number of colors; this should be stated explicitly. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))

[n] should be defined as the discrete interval {1,...,n}, and ms([n],r) is a normalized quantity (equivalently MS(n,r)/n), not the raw cardinality invariant MS(n,r). ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))

The relevant symmetry on both [n] and [0,1] is central symmetry: in the discrete model x -> g-x with integer g, and in the continuous model x -> c-x with real center c. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))

ms([0,1],r) is defined via measurable r-colorings of [0,1] with Lebesgue measure and measurable monochromatic centrally symmetric subsets; the measure-theoretic setup is part of the meaning of the notation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))

bms([n],r) is the blurred invariant, defined by taking the infimum over blurred r-colorings rather than ordinary colorings; without saying this, the second sequence is not stand-alone. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))

The convergence variable is n -> infinity, and the paper's context shows that both ms([n],r) and bms([n],r) approximate ms([0,1],r) from above. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v7i1r52/pdf/))

The paper's intended sharpening is not merely 'determine how fast' in an informal sense, but specifically to obtain an error estimate, with the source asking whether there exists alpha>0 such that |ms([n],r)-ms([0,1],r)| = O(1/n^alpha), and then to compare that with the convergence speed of bms([n],r). ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v7i1r52/pdf/))
refined_question: For a fixed integer r>=1, let [n]={1,...,n} be equipped with normalized counting measure and central symmetries x -> g-x (g in Z), and let [0,1] be equipped with Lebesgue measure and central symmetries x -> c-x (c in R). Let ms([n],r) denote the normalized maximal size of a monochromatic centrally symmetric subset guaranteed in every r-coloring of [n], and let bms([n],r) denote the corresponding blurred invariant. Since ms([n],r) -> ms([0,1],r) and bms([n],r) -> ms([0,1],r) as n -> infinity, determine the rate of convergence of these sequences to ms([0,1],r); in particular, does there exist alpha>0 such that |ms([n],r)-ms([0,1],r)| = O(1/n^alpha), and does bms([n],r) converge asymptotically faster than ms([n],r)? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))
justification: The draft is aimed at the end-of-section interval problem in Section 8, not at the earlier group-theoretic questions. The survey's official wording in Question 8.5 is terse, so making it stand-alone requires importing the interval-specific definitions of ms and bms from the immediately preceding Section 8 context together with the general measured-space definition of ms from Sections 5-6. The survey itself asks only 'How quickly...?', but the underlying source cited there shows the intended concrete rate benchmark O(1/n^alpha) and the comparison with the blurred invariant, which is the sharpest paper-faithful way to rewrite your draft without broadening it. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/0901.3356))
